title: God's Wrath and Vengeance
hook: If God is not cruel, what are his wrath and vengeance for?
tldr: God's wrath is not emotional rage but withdrawn protection, letting people face the consequences of their choices, aimed at repentance. His vengeance purges impurity and restores, as Isaiah 1 shows. Unlike human revenge, divine wrath is measured, temporary, corrective and constructive.
big_idea: God's wrath corrects and purifies; it never aims to destroy forever.

points.title: Not soft on sin
points.text: God is slow to anger yet visits iniquity to the third and fourth generation. This is no hypergrace theory; sin has real consequences.

points.title: Egypt's plagues brought converts
points.text: The plagues aimed first at repentance. A mixed multitude of Egyptians left their idols and joined Israel by faith; wrath was a call for change.

points.title: Wrath is withdrawn protection
points.text: God's wrath meant letting people face their choices. When Israel trusted other gods, he stopped defending them and pagan nations attacked.

points.title: The Lord disciplines those he loves
points.text: Like the Prodigal's father letting his son learn from his choices, God's discipline is purposeful and redemptive, meant to purify and grow us.

points.title: Vengeance purges dross and restores
points.text: In Isaiah, God vents wrath on his foes to purge their dross, restore their leaders and make Jerusalem the Faithful City.

sections.summary: If not on Jesus, where does God's wrath go? We all shout penalty at a foul on TV, wanting fairness, and God is slow to anger yet visits iniquity to the fourth generation. God is not soft on sin, against hypergrace. Yet wrath is not vengeance and hatred. The plagues of Egypt, parallel to Revelation's, aimed at repentance: multitudes of Egyptians abandoned idols to join Israel by faith.

sections.h: Judgment as a call to harvest
sections.summary: We tend to imagine Egypt's plagues as Marvel Studios-style vengeance, but they brought Egyptians into saving faith. God's wrath was a call for change. The great judgment and tribulation should be seen not as mere retribution but as mercy, a call for a harvest of people to believe.

Ancient audiences linked wrath to disasters and upheavals. Wrath means letting people face their sins' consequences. It is not human, immature anger but the natural outcome of leaving God's path, like the Prodigal's father letting his son learn. When Israel worshiped other gods, God did not strike with lightning or lava; he withdrew protection and cruel pagan nations attacked.

As a rule, Old Testament wrath is God letting wicked pagans overcome Israel without defending them, matching the Law's curses. It is as if God said, let's see how the other gods treat you. Pagans often forced Israel to worship their gods, gods who demanded children be burned. The Lord disciplines those he loves: wrath is purposeful and redemptive, purifying and maturing.

People judge harshly to feel superior or cope with insecurity. Hollywood images of bloody apocalypse suggest revenge is godly, but true divinity lies in empathy and forgiveness. Paul says leave vengeance to God's wrath. Isaiah 1:24-26 shows its purpose: God avenges himself on his foes by purging their dross, restoring their leaders and calling them the City of Righteousness, the Faithful City.

sections.h: Why we leave revenge to God
sections.summary: Divine vengeance aims to discipline and restore the transgressor, not crush or condemn forever, unlike human revenge fueled by rage. God exposes wrongs to inspire healing through grace, not wrathful judgment. If we retaliate, they retaliate in an endless circle; if we don't, God can activate his justice. His judgment exposes truth so the issue can be treated and healed: to correct, not condemn.

Human wrath is often cruel, merciless and destructive. God's wrath, the biblical term for disciplining Israel, was always measured, temporary, corrective and constructive. It expresses his deep commitment to justice, righteousness and the welfare of creation, aiming to rectify unjust and oppressive behavior and restore harmony and prosperity.

mythfact.myth: God's wrath is like Marvel-style vengeance raining fire from the sky.
mythfact.fact: In the Old Testament, wrath usually meant God withdrawing protection, letting pagan nations attack when Israel turned to other gods.

mythfact.myth: Rejecting eternal hell means God is soft on sin.
mythfact.fact: God visits iniquity to the third and fourth generation; his wrath is real but measured, temporary and corrective.

mythfact.myth: God's vengeance aims to destroy his enemies forever.
mythfact.fact: Isaiah 1:24-26 shows vengeance purging dross and restoring, so the city becomes the Faithful City.

terms.meaning: God's measured, temporary discipline, often withdrawing protection so people face the consequences of their choices.
A popular theory treating God as soft on sin, which the source explicitly rejects.
God's repayment of wrongs, aimed at purifying and restoring the transgressor rather than condemning forever.

quiz.q: How was God's wrath usually expressed against Israel in the Old Testament?
options: Lightning and lava from the sky
quiz.why: God withdrew protection, letting pagan nations attack when Israel worshiped other gods.

quiz.q: What happened to many Egyptians after the plagues?
quiz.why: Exodus 12:38 says multitudes of Egyptians joined Israel, abandoning their idols; the plagues called for change.

quiz.q: In Isaiah 1:24-26, what is the result of God's vengeance?
quiz.why: God purges dross, restores leaders, and the city becomes the City of Righteousness, the Faithful City.

reflect: When you are wronged, do you want the offender destroyed or restored, and which looks more like God?
